proposed_value:
- E1 and E2 enhancer classes differ in biochemical features: E1 shows stronger H3K27ac, DNase I hypersensitivity, and AP-1 factor binding (JUN, ATF3) compared to E2, which exhibits weaker but still detectable activity (Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). 
- E1 sequences have stronger gene expression effects in CRISPR perturbation experiments, even after controlling for 3D contact (Extended Data Fig. 6e), and are more likely to be predicted as enhancers in K562 cells (94% vs. 49%) and broadly active across cell types (32% of E1 vs. 13% of E2 predicted as ABC enhancers in >50 of 130 biosamples).
- E1 enhancers are significantly enriched for FOS and JUN motifs, while E2 enhancers show no significant motif enrichment (Benjamini-Hochberg corrected P < 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 6b,c), and both classes produce enhancer RNAs (GRO-cap) and show similar sequence conservation (Extended Data Fig. 6g,h).
- Despite differences in genomic activity, E1 and E2 sequences show similar average activity in ExP-STARR-seq assays (Extended Data Fig. 4b), suggesting potential assay-specific artifacts, such as episomal sequences affecting reporter expression through non-transcriptional mechanisms or detecting activity not reflected in chromosomal context (references 16, 17, 29). 
- The study includes 65 genes with previously studied enhancers in CRISPR experiments in K562 cells (ref. 22), 715 genes spanning a range of promoter activities (including top 200 expressed genes by CAGE and 515 random expressed genes >1 TPM), and 20 genes not expressed in K562 but active in GM12878 and HCT-116 (top 70% by TPM in RNA-seq).
rationale:
- E1 and E2 classes differ in genomic features: E1 shows stronger H3K27ac, DNase I hypersensitivity, and AP-1 binding (Extended Data Fig. 6a–d).
- E1 sequences are more active in CRISPR experiments and more broadly predicted as enhancers across cell types (32% vs. 13% in >50 biosamples).
- E1 is enriched for FOS/JUN motifs; both classes produce eRNAs and show similar conservation (Extended Data Fig. 6g,h).
